Red flags: 2025 dismissal of the director after misconduct reports
- Kris Callens, director since 2015, left the Fries Museum on 1 February 2025. The museum officially cited a reorganisation; the same week it emerged that several women had complained about his boundary-crossing behaviour (NOS with Omrop Fryslân, 16 March 2025).
- Supervisory board chair Hayo Apotheker said the first report came in December 2024 and the confidential counsellor received nine reports, not all of them about sexual misconduct; no one filed a formal complaint. He said dismissal was already being considered because of financial problems and a planned reorganisation, and the reports removed any remaining doubts (NOS, 16 March 2025).
- The Leeuwarder Courant spoke with more than 70 current and former employees, witnesses and others in the cultural sector (NOS, 16 March 2025).
- The union Kunstenbond asked for an external investigation into misconduct at the museum during Callens' time as director; the supervisory board did not support one (NOS, 16 March 2025).
- On 21 March 2025 the museum confirmed that Callens left after reports of sexual and boundary-crossing misconduct, said "We zijn geschrokken van hun verhalen" ("We were shocked by their stories", translated), and said more openness from the start "was de betere keuze geweest" ("would have been the better choice", translated). It said it was considering an independent investigation (VRT NWS, 21 March 2025).
- When Callens left, the museum had cited "teruggeschroefde subsidies en financiële problemen" ("reduced subsidies and financial problems", translated) (VRT NWS, 21 March 2025). The article carries no statement from Callens.

Red flags: 2022 to 2025 cost overrun on the redevelopment
- In March 2022 the cost of the gallery's redevelopment rose by about $9.4 million to $64.4 million, which the Whanganui District Council might need to fund; the delays were put down to Covid-19, supply chains and earthquake strengthening of the 1919 building (Whanganui Chronicle, 10 March 2022).
- Councillor Philippa Baker-Hogan said residents struggling with living costs would be badly affected if they had to cover the "cost blow-out"; councillor Hadleigh Reid called the extra costs disappointing after a thorough planning process. Councillor Helen Craig replied: "You can't leave a building partly finished" (Whanganui Chronicle, Jacob McSweeny, 11 March 2022).
- The final cost was $79.4 million against an original budget of $55.06 million, an overspend of $19.67 million, with the work extended by 21 months. The council's share is $26.08 million, including its original $5 million commitment (RNZ, Local Democracy Reporting, 1 August 2025).
- Mayor Andrew Tripe called a ratepayer share of about a third "an extraordinary outcome", and chief executive David Langford said the project was "completed to a high standard" (RNZ, 1 August 2025).

Red flags: 2024 proposed council cut to operating funding
- In its draft Long Term Plan 2024 to 2034 the Whanganui District Council proposed cutting $200,000 a year from the gallery's operating funding. Sarjeant Gallery Trust chairwoman Nicola Williams said she was "flabbergasted" and that the cut would "send the worst signal to our benefactors"; the council said the gallery's draft 2024/25 operating budget was about $400,000 higher than first planned, mainly because of insurance and energy costs (Whanganui Chronicle, Mike Tweed, 17 May 2024).
